title: Dome 7: Plants on Strike
hook: The greenhouse has tons of light and CO2. So why did the plants stop making sugar?
briefing: Your plants run two machines. The light machine splits water and makes ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle spends them so Rubisco can turn CO2 into sugar. The whole thing only runs as fast as its scarcest supply.
intro: Alarms! Dome 7's oxygen maker just died, and the greenhouse is now your only air. A power surge locked everything. Fix the light room, fix the carbon bay, then crack the airlock.
outro_win: The airlock hisses open. The plants are back to work, and you can breathe again. Nice botany, hero.
outro_lose: Time's up, and the plants are still sulking. Check the Field Guide, retry the locks you missed, and go again.

checks.prompt: The cabinet only opens for the flask that got heavy-oxygen WATER. Which flask was it?
hints: Check the Tracer lab notebook. Compare the mass of the O2 from each flask.
Photosystem II splits water to replace its lost electrons. Whose oxygen atoms end up in the O2 gas?
Similar case: if CO2 made the O2, the heavy-CO2 flask would give heavy O2 (mass 36). Use that logic on the real data.
options: Both flasks, because O2 comes from water and CO2 equally
Neither flask, because heavy oxygen would end up in the sugar

wrong_feedback.feedback: Flask B gave normal O2 (mass 32). Picked it? You may think O2 comes from CO2. Which molecule does Photosystem II split?

wrong_feedback.option: Both flasks, because O2 comes from water and CO2 equally
wrong_feedback.feedback: If both counted, both flasks would show heavy O2. Only one did. CO2's oxygen ends up in sugar and water, not O2 gas.

wrong_feedback.option: Neither flask, because heavy oxygen would end up in the sugar
wrong_feedback.feedback: True for CO2's oxygen! But one flask clearly gave heavy O2 (mass 36). Where did that come from?

checks.prompt: The frozen turbine wants a number: how many times more H+ is in the thylakoid lumen than in the stroma? Enter it.
hints: Read the pH probe display. It shows the lumen and the stroma.
Lower pH means more H+. Each 1-unit pH step is 10 times more H+. That stored gradient is what spins ATP synthase.
Similar example: pH 4 has 10 x 10 = 100 times more H+ than pH 6. Now try it with the probe's readings.

checks.prompt: The breaker won't flush bay 2 until you prove the DCMU leak. Which bay 2 reading proves it?
hints: Re-read the tag on the breaker panel. It names the exact hand-off DCMU blocks.
Photosystem II only keeps splitting water while it can pass its electrons on. Block that, and what stops first?
Similar case: jam a factory's exit belt and the machines feeding it stop too, even with the power on. What feeds Photosystem II its electrons?
options: Light absorption drops to zero, because DCMU destroys chlorophyll
CO2 uptake stops but O2 release continues at full speed
No readings change, because Photosystem I can still absorb light
O2 release drops to zero, because water splitting has nowhere to send its electrons
answer: O2 release drops to zero, because water splitting has nowhere to send its electrons

wrong_feedback.option: Light absorption drops to zero, because DCMU destroys chlorophyll
wrong_feedback.feedback: The tag says DCMU blocks an electron hand-off. It doesn't touch pigments, so chlorophyll still absorbs light.

wrong_feedback.option: CO2 uptake stops but O2 release continues at full speed
wrong_feedback.feedback: O2 comes from splitting water at Photosystem II. If PSII can't pass electrons on, can it keep splitting water?

wrong_feedback.option: No readings change, because Photosystem I can still absorb light
wrong_feedback.feedback: Photosystem I needs electrons from Photosystem II. Block the line upstream and everything stalls.

checks.prompt: The hatch wants exactly enough CO2 to export 5 G3P as sugar. How many CO2 must enter the Calvin cycle?
hints: Use the Calvin cycle ledger. Compare the CO2 that went in with the G3P exported.
Most G3P is recycled to rebuild RuBP. Only the net G3P leaves as sugar. Each exported G3P has 3 carbons, and each carbon came from one CO2.
Similar example: exporting 2 G3P takes 2 x 3 = 6 CO2, just like the ledger shows. Scale it up.

checks.prompt: The vent controller wants a diagnosis. Why is sugar output falling when the lights are on full?
hints: Read the Air-mix gauge. Check the O2, the CO2, and the stomata.
Rubisco can grab O2 instead of CO2. High O2 and low CO2 make that happen way more often, which wastes carbon and ATP.
Similar case: a cashier who grabs the top coin grabs the wrong coin more when wrong coins pile up. What's piling up in the dome?
options: The plants are using the extra O2 for cellular respiration and burning their sugar faster than they make it
Rubisco is grabbing O2 instead of CO2 (photorespiration), wasting carbon and ATP
The light reactions have stopped because there is not enough CO2 for them to split
The high O2 is bleaching the chlorophyll so it can no longer absorb light
answer: Rubisco is grabbing O2 instead of CO2 (photorespiration), wasting carbon and ATP

wrong_feedback.option: The plants are using the extra O2 for cellular respiration and burning their sugar faster than they make it
wrong_feedback.feedback: Extra O2 doesn't speed up respiration like this. The gauge points at the carbon-fixing enzyme. What does Rubisco do when O2 is high?

wrong_feedback.option: The high O2 is bleaching the chlorophyll so it can no longer absorb light
wrong_feedback.feedback: The lights are fine, and there's no sign of pigment damage. The problem is on the carbon-fixing side.

wrong_feedback.option: The light reactions have stopped because there is not enough CO2 for them to split
wrong_feedback.feedback: The light reactions split water, not CO2. Rubisco uses CO2 in the Calvin cycle.

checks.prompt: Final lock! Use your fragments: the ATP output, the NADPH output, and the cost of one CO2. How many CO2 per minute can the Calvin cycle really fix?
hints: Check your collected fragments. You have both supply rates and the cost of each CO2.
Work out how many CO2 each supply could pay for alone. A process runs only as fast as its scarcest input.
Similar example: 20 eggs and 10 cups of flour, with 2 eggs and 1 cup per cake, make min(20/2, 10/1) = 10 cakes. Do the same with ATP and NADPH.

content.premise: You're the botanist on Mars station Dome 7. The oxygen maker is dead, and the station has 20 minutes of air left. Every greenhouse system is locked. The locks only open for someone who knows how plants really work. No pressure.

rooms.name: Light Reactor Control Room
rooms.description: Algae tanks glow under grow lamps. Three consoles blink angry red: a sample cabinet, the ATP synthase housing, and the breaker panel.

hotspots.label: Tracer lab notebook
hotspots.description: Day 212: two identical algae flasks got heavy oxygen (18O), one in its water and one in its CO2. The surge smeared the labels. O2 gas readout: Flask A = mass 36 (heavy). Flask B = mass 32 (normal).

hotspots.label: Sealed sample cabinet
hotspots.reveals_clue: Water tank full: water is NOT the bottleneck.
hotspots.description: It holds the two mystery flasks. The keypad blinks: WHICH ONE DRANK THE HEAVY WATER?

hotspots.label: pH probe display
hotspots.description: Two probes poke into a chloroplast. Sticker: each 1-unit pH drop = 10 times more H+, and ATP synthase only spins while H+ flows down its gradient. Readout: lumen pH 5. Stroma pH 8.

hotspots.label: ATP synthase housing
hotspots.reveals_clue: Turbine spinning! Meter: ATP output = 21 per minute.
hotspots.description: A turbine-shaped ATP synthase, frozen mid-spin. Its screen wants the gradient strength.

hotspots.label: Electron-flow breaker panel
hotspots.reveals_clue: Bay 2 flushed! Meter: NADPH output = 16 per minute.
hotspots.description: Tag: "Weed-killer DCMU leaked into bay 2. It stops plastoquinone from taking electrons from Photosystem II." Bay 2 sensors: light absorption, O2 release, CO2 uptake.

rooms.name: Carbon Fixation Bay
rooms.description: Leafy racks fill a sticky, humid bay. The air tastes stale. The export hatch, the air vent, and the airlock are all sealed.

hotspots.label: Calvin cycle ledger
hotspots.description: Batch record: 6 CO2 went in, and Rubisco stuck each one onto RuBP. The cycle used 18 ATP and 12 NADPH to make 12 G3P: 10 rebuilt 6 RuBP, and 2 left as sugar.

hotspots.label: Sugar export hatch
hotspots.reveals_clue: Footnote: each CO2 fixed costs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH.
hotspots.description: This hatch feeds sugar to the very hungry station kitchen. Screen: LOAD CO2 FOR 5 EXPORTED G3P.

hotspots.label: Air-mix gauge
hotspots.description: The gauge flashes like it's panicking. Readout: O2 38%, CO2 0.01%, leaf temp 35 C, stomata closed, lights full, sugar output falling.

hotspots.label: Air vent controller
hotspots.reveals_clue: Vent open! No more photorespiration: every Rubisco reaction fixes CO2.
hotspots.description: A jammed vent to the station's air scrubber. It won't budge until you name the problem.

hotspots.label: Airlock
hotspots.description: The only way out. Panel: ENTER TRUE CARBON-FIXATION RATE (CO2 per minute). Use your fragments.

field_guide.title: Photolysis (water splitting)
field_guide.explanation: Photosystem II splits water to replace the electrons it loses. The oxygen from that water becomes the O2 gas plants release.

field_guide.title: Linear electron flow
field_guide.explanation: Electrons go from Photosystem II through plastoquinone, the cytochrome complex, and plastocyanin to Photosystem I, then to NADP+ to make NADPH. Block any hand-off and the whole line stalls.

field_guide.title: Chemiosmosis in the chloroplast
field_guide.explanation: The electron chain pumps H+ into the thylakoid lumen. When H+ flows back out through ATP synthase, it spins it and makes ATP.

field_guide.title: Calvin cycle
field_guide.explanation: In the stroma, Rubisco sticks CO2 onto RuBP. ATP and NADPH turn the product into G3P, and most G3P rebuilds RuBP. Each CO2 costs 3 ATP and 2 NADPH, and 3 CO2 make one exported G3P.

field_guide.title: Rubisco and photorespiration
field_guide.explanation: Rubisco can grab O2 instead of CO2, especially when it's hot, O2 is high, and CO2 is low. That wastes carbon and ATP and makes no sugar.

field_guide.title: Limiting factors
field_guide.explanation: A process runs only as fast as its scarcest input. Linear flow alone makes slightly too little ATP, so chloroplasts top it up with cyclic electron flow.
